fullTitle: World Model Based Robotic Sorting with a Physical Leader and Follower Arm
subtitle: Track 1 · Physical AI with LeRobot arms

pages.text:
Physical AI Hackathon
World model control and human video driven humanoid learning
This brief defines two college hackathon challenges. Teams will build systems that learn from demonstrations, perform color based object sorting, and demonstrate measurable performance under changes to the scene. Track 1 uses a physical leader and follower robot arm. Track 2 uses a simulated humanoid in NVIDIA Isaac Sim and Isaac Lab.
The two challenges
Track
Challenge
Required result
1
World model based robotic sorting
A physical arm sorts three colored cubes into matching bins and uses learned future prediction to choose or refine actions.
2
Human video to humanoid skill adaptation
A pipeline converts newly recorded human demonstrations into useful training supervision and improves a simulated humanoid sorting policy.
Recommended event format
Use a two week preparation window followed by a 72 hour build event. Teams of 3 to 5 students choose one track. A 48 hour edition is feasible only when organizers supply working environments, compatible checkpoints, starter data and tested robot interfaces. Training a large foundation model from scratch is outside the core scope.
How to use this brief
Participant requirements are defined in the track sections. Proposed counts, time limits, workspace dimensions and scoring rules are event design choices, not hardware or model guarantees. Organizers must validate and freeze them before registration. No particular commercial hardware supplier or college affiliation is required.
Technical references were checked on 14 November 2026. Pin the exact software versions, model revisions and asset licenses for the event rather than installing moving development branches.
1 Shared scope and terminology
LeRobot and the physical platform
LeRobot is the Hugging Face robotics software ecosystem, rather than a single robot model. For this event, a compatible SO 101 leader and follower arm pair is a reference platform; equivalent approved hardware is acceptable. The leader records demonstrations through teleoperation. The follower must execute autonomously during judged trials. [1][2]
What counts as a world model
For Track 1, a world model must learn how task relevant state changes over time, conditioned on candidate robot actions. It may predict images, latent features, object poses, contact state or combinations of these. The predictions must influence planning, action ranking, policy improvement or runtime action generation. A simulator alone, a language model giving instructions, or color detection with fixed trajectories does not satisfy this requirement.
ACT and SmolVLA may be comparison baselines or action proposal modules, but an unchanged imitation policy alone does not qualify as the Track 1 solution. Robustness is evaluated separately: using a world model does not guarantee generalization.
Model options
A compact learned dynamics model with model predictive control is an acceptable and practical route. An approved pretrained world action model is also acceptable. AW 0, meaning Agentic World Action Models, is a research reference for combining predictive modeling and robot actions; its use is optional and depends on verified checkpoint access, embodiment support and compute. No team is required to reproduce the full research system. [3][4]
GR00T and humanoid control
Track 2 targets a pinned NVIDIA Isaac GR00T N1.5 or N1.6 checkpoint compatible with the supplied embodiment. GR00T is used for task policy adaptation. Organizers must separately provide a tested standing and locomotion controller, controller interface and robot asset. Loading a task foundation model does not by itself establish safe walking or balance. [5][6]
Meaning of training in Isaac
All Track 2 robot interaction, synthetic trajectory generation and scored rollouts occur in Isaac Sim through the supplied Isaac Lab environment. Video processing and neural network optimization may run as external Python or PyTorch jobs connected to this workflow. They need not run inside the simulator application. [7]

2 Track 1 problem statement
Build an autonomous robotic sorting system that uses a learned world model to pick up red, green and blue cubes and place each cube into the matching colored bin. Collect demonstrations with a leader and follower setup using LeRobot or an approved equivalent. The system must observe the current scene, predict relevant consequences of candidate actions, execute a short action segment, observe again and continue until sorting is complete.
Reference workspace
One securely mounted follower arm and one leader arm for demonstrations; one tabletop with three bins and three cubes, one cube per color.
One fixed RGB camera covering the workspace. A wrist camera or RGB D camera is optional, provided all teams have equivalent access for scoring.
Suggested cubes are lightweight matte blocks approximately 30 to 40 mm wide. Select the final size only after verifying gripper aperture, payload, grasp clearance and camera visibility.
Bins must provide ample placement clearance and be reachable without collision. Organizers publish tested source and destination regions and a safe arm home pose.
Required behavior
Given the instruction “Place each cube in the bin of the same color,” identify a cube, grasp it, lift it clear of the table, transport it to its matching bin, release it and continue. Cube and bin order must be inferred from observations rather than a memorized left to right sequence. A release beside a bin or a placement into the wrong color does not count.
Changes the system must handle
Evaluation includes randomized cube locations, reordered bins, moderate lighting variation, changed tabletop appearance and a relocated arm base. Every scene must remain mechanically reachable and visually solvable. Base relocation happens only between trials, with power and motion disabled, followed by secure remounting and the permitted calibration procedure.
Minimum qualifying submission
Submit an autonomous physical demonstration, trained world model or adapted checkpoint, future prediction evidence, logs showing how predictions affect action choice, and held out evaluation results. A video prediction demo without robot control, a fixed movement replay or a standalone ACT or SmolVLA policy is incomplete.
3 Track 1 components and implementation
Component
Purpose and required preparation
Robot and interfaces
Leader and follower, gripper, approved power supply, motor interface, cables and rigid clamps. Verify firmware, calibration and joint limits before the event.
Observation and geometry
RGB camera, timestamps, robot state, camera intrinsics and camera to robot transform when needed. Use depth or fiducials only under published common rules.
Learning stack
Pinned LeRobot, Python, PyTorch, OpenCV and dataset tools. Add a custom world model adapter if the selected model lacks native LeRobot integration.
World model
Learn action conditioned transitions in visual latent or object state space, or adapt an approved pretrained world action model.
Planner and control
Candidate action generation, predicted outcome scoring, bounded execution and replanning. IK, collision checks and safety limits may support execution.
Logging
Episode records, action timestamps, predictions, chosen actions, actual outcomes, failures and checkpoint identity.
Suggested compact architecture
Encode camera observations and joint state into a task state. Predict the next state from the current state and a candidate action sequence. Sample candidate gripper motions, score predicted grasp and placement progress along with collision risk, execute the first short segment and replan. Teams choose the prediction horizon and control rate based on measured hardware latency.
An object state world model is valid if its transition function is learned and evaluated. A detector followed only by analytic IK and hardcoded rules is a useful baseline but does not meet the world model requirement. Fixed low level safety controllers are allowed.
Training evidence
Provide the objective, action representation, normalization, prediction horizon and trainable parameter count. Evaluate future prediction on held out episodes. Compare at least two candidate actions from the same observation and show that the predicted outcomes differ meaningfully. Include examples of both correct and incorrect predictions.
Suggested collection budget
Start with 60 to 120 complete sorting episodes across varied layouts, or a smaller approved starter set plus team collected additions. These are planning targets, not a guaranteed sufficient dataset. Include grasp failures and recovery attempts with explicit outcome labels. Split by full episode and scene configuration; adjacent frames from the same recording must not cross training and test sets.
4 Track 1 generalization and evaluation
Condition
Held out trials
Controlled variation
A Standard scene
5
New cube and bin arrangements on the familiar surface.
B Lighting
5
Different diffuse brightness or light direction; colors remain distinguishable and images usable.
C Table appearance
5
A different matte surface, texture or background with comparable geometry.
D Base relocation
5
Arm translated or rotated within an organizer validated mounting zone; all objects remain reachable.
E Combined changes
5
Layout plus moderate lighting and surface variation; no additional training.
Trial protocol
Freeze weights and code before the 25 scored trials. Judges provide the same seeded scenes or matched physical arrangements to all teams. Each trial starts from home with three unsorted cubes and lasts at most 120 seconds. The timer begins with the task command. Teams may retry grasps autonomously within this time. No leader control, manual scene assistance or hidden remote operator is allowed.
For relocation, allow a common setup interval of up to 3 minutes before the timed run for automatic pose estimation or a disclosed geometric calibration routine. No new demonstrations, gradient updates or hand entered target coordinates are permitted. Record calibration duration separately. If organizers add a stricter no recalibration award, score it separately rather than mixing protocols.
Success and failures
A cube succeeds when fully released into its correct bin and remains inside for 2 seconds. A trial succeeds when all three cubes succeed within the time limit with no intervention. Wrong bin placements count only if autonomously corrected before timeout. Out of workspace drops, hard collisions or emergency stops end the trial; already verified placements remain recorded but the trial is a failure.
Metrics
Cube accuracy is correct cubes divided by 75. Full task success is completed trials divided by 25. Report both per condition, plus completion time on successful trials, retry count, emergency stops and planning latency. Do not report timeouts as fast completions. Report robustness as the mean full task success across conditions B to E, with the corresponding counts.
World model ablation
Run 10 separate paired scenes using the full system and a prediction disabled baseline under the same action budget and initial conditions. Disable learned lookahead while retaining the remaining pipeline where feasible. These runs are additional to the 25 scored trials. Report all outcomes even if the world model does not improve success; a negative result does not justify suppressing trials.

World model control and human video driven humanoid learning

Track 1 uses a physical leader and follower robot arm. Track 2 uses a simulated humanoid in NVIDIA Isaac Sim and Isaac Lab.
The two challenges
Track
Challenge
Required result
1
World model based robotic sorting
A physical arm sorts three colored cubes into matching bins and uses learned future prediction to choose or refine actions.
2
Human video to humanoid skill adaptation
A pipeline converts newly recorded human demonstrations into useful training supervision and improves a simulated humanoid sorting policy.

A 48 hour edition is feasible only when organizers supply working environments, compatible checkpoints, starter data and tested robot interfaces. It may predict images, latent features, object poses, contact state or combinations of these. The predictions must influence planning, action ranking, policy improvement or runtime action generation. A simulator alone, a language model giving instructions, or color detection with fixed trajectories does not satisfy this requirement.
ACT and SmolVLA may be comparison baselines or action proposal modules, but an unchanged imitation policy alone does not qualify as the Track 1 solution. Robustness is evaluated separately: using a world model does not guarantee generalization.
Model options
A compact learned dynamics model with model predictive control is an acceptable and practical route. An approved pretrained world action model is also acceptable. AW 0, meaning Agentic World Action Models, is a research reference for combining predictive modeling and robot actions; its use is optional and depends on verified checkpoint access, embodiment support and compute. No team is required to reproduce the full research system. [3][4]
GR00T and humanoid control
Track 2 targets a pinned NVIDIA Isaac GR00T N1.5 or N1.6 checkpoint compatible with the supplied embodiment. GR00T is used for task policy adaptation. Organizers must separately provide a tested standing and locomotion controller, controller interface and robot asset. Loading a task foundation model does not by itself establish safe walking or balance. [5][6]
Meaning of training in Isaac
All Track 2 robot interaction, synthetic trajectory generation and scored rollouts occur in Isaac Sim through the supplied Isaac Lab environment. Video processing and neural network optimization may run as external Python or PyTorch jobs connected to this workflow. They need not run inside the simulator application. [7]

5 Track 2 problem statement
Build a reproducible pipeline that uses newly recorded human video demonstrations to post train a pretrained humanoid task policy. In NVIDIA Isaac Sim and Isaac Lab, the humanoid must pick up colored cubes from a table and sort them into three matching bins or designated receiving zones. The submission must show that information extracted from the team’s human demonstrations contributed to training and changed the policy’s behavior.
Reference simulated task
Use one organizer supplied humanoid with a tested manipulation interface, three colored cubes, three matching bins and a table at a reachable height. The humanoid starts standing at a marked pose. A complete episode requires grasping and sorting all three cubes without falling, losing objects outside the workspace or relying on privileged object poses during policy evaluation.
Standing and walking scope
Core scoring measures stable standing and manipulation at the table. Before the task demo, show a short operation of the organizer supplied standing and walking controller, such as walking between two marked points in a separate clear scene. This is an integration check, not a requirement to learn walking from sorting videos. Walking to the table and transitioning into manipulation is a stretch goal using the same supplied controller.
Human demonstration task
A person performs the same sorting task with the same color mapping using physical cubes and bins. Record first person video with a phone or head mounted camera, or third person video with a fixed phone or camera. Either view qualifies for core scoring; using both is optional. The recording should clearly show hands, objects, approach, grasp, transfer and release.
Required learning result
Use the supplied GR00T N1.5 or N1.6 checkpoint and compatible action representation, with an approved embodiment adapter when necessary. Demonstrate a real optimization step on useful task supervision and evaluate the resulting checkpoint against its starting checkpoint. A language prompt change, replayed animation or fully scripted sorting controller does not count as post training.
Optional extension
Add a fourth yellow bin and cube, category based sorting, or approach and sort behavior only after the three color core task works. Keep extension results separate so teams remain comparable. A different task requires organizer approval and must preserve the human video to training to autonomous behavior requirement.
6 Track 2 video to robot learning pipeline
Human video contains visual motion but usually lacks robot joint commands, gripper commands and calibrated metric depth. Teams must explain and implement the bridge from these observations to robot training targets. Directly relabeling human wrist motion as humanoid joint actions is not a valid conversion.
Stage 1 Record and curate
Suggested starting budget is 30 to 60 complete demonstrations across at least 10 layouts, with 5 to 15 seconds of usable video per cube transfer. Capture at 1080p and 30 frames per second or better when available. Retain source timestamps, view type, task labels, participant consent, clip boundaries and failure annotations. Avoid collecting unnecessary faces, audio or personal information.
Stage 2 Extract task structure
Detect or segment cubes and bins, track object and hand motion, and identify phases such as approach, grasp, lift, transfer and release. Optional hand pose estimators can support this process. Recover camera geometry or normalized table coordinates using calibration targets or known dimensions. Monocular scale ambiguity and occlusion must be addressed rather than ignored.
Stage 3 Build feasible robot supervision
Recommended route: infer object goals, phase order and approximate end effector paths from human videos; transform these into simulator coordinates; solve robot specific IK and grasp constraints; generate and validate trajectories in Isaac. Reject unreachable or colliding targets and unstable motions. Record synchronized simulated observations, robot states, actions and task instructions from successful executions.
Alternative route: use human video for representation or task progress learning and combine it with a disclosed robot demonstration set for the action head. This qualifies only if human derived supervision affects trainable parameters used by the final controller and its contribution is tested. Simulator demonstrations alone, unrelated to human recordings, do not satisfy the track.
Stage 4 Adapt and deploy
Export compatible training episodes, define embodiment modalities and normalization, and fine tune the selected GR00T checkpoint using its supported recipe. Adapter training or partial freezing is allowed only when supported by the pinned release. Run closed loop inference against Isaac observations and route task actions through the tested humanoid controller.
Stage 5 Establish contribution
Evaluate the starting checkpoint, the final adapted checkpoint and a matched training run without human derived supervision. Keep robot data budget, compute budget and evaluation seeds as similar as possible. State any unavoidable mismatch. Show the provenance of at least one human clip through extracted targets, simulated trajectories, training records and final evaluation.
7 Track 2 technologies and data contract
Layer
Required role and possible tools
Simulation
NVIDIA Isaac Sim for scene physics and rendering; Isaac Lab for task reset, observation, action and evaluation orchestration. Use the organizer pinned compatible versions.
Robot policy
GR00T N1.5 or N1.6 checkpoint with exact revision, supported fine tuning recipe and an embodiment specific modality configuration.
Locomotion and balance
Organizer validated controller and motion interface. Task actions must coexist with balance and joint limits; do not assume arbitrary upper body targets are stable.
Video processing
Python and OpenCV for frame processing; approved object, hand or pose estimators with documented licenses. Tools are options, not mandatory dependencies.
Retargeting
Camera and table transforms, metric scale estimation, IK, joint limits, contact aware grasp planning and simulator feasibility checks.
Training and tracking
PyTorch, supported model dependencies, checkpoint storage, training curves, config files and deterministic dataset manifests.
Minimum episode fields
Each robot training episode must contain an episode identifier, timestamps, task instruction, camera streams, robot state, action targets, success label, termination reason and provenance links to the source demonstration. Record joint ordering, units, coordinate frames, action timing and gripper convention. Use the schema expected by the pinned model release; LeRobot format may be used when supported by that release.
Provenance and quality checks
Preserve source clip identifier, extraction version, calibration, human derived targets, retargeting configuration and resulting simulator episode identifiers.
Verify monotonic timestamps, aligned observations and actions, consistent dimensions, finite numeric values and no training and test scene overlap.
Distinguish simulator ground truth used to generate supervision from policy inputs. Judges may use simulator state for scoring; the evaluated policy uses approved cameras and proprioception.
Report rejected trajectories and why they failed, including IK errors, collision, poor grasp, unstable posture or uncertain video interpretation.
Required integration proof
Provide a saved task policy checkpoint, a training log showing parameter updates and loss progression, and a rollout driven by that checkpoint. Retargeted motion playback can demonstrate dataset construction but is not the final autonomous policy demonstration.
8 Track 2 evaluation and judging
Freeze model weights, scene code and inference configuration before evaluation. Run 30 episodes using organizer held out seeds: 10 standard randomized layouts, 10 unseen cube and bin arrangements, and 10 moderate lighting and table appearance changes. Each episode has three cubes and a 180 second simulated time limit. Report wall clock time and real time factor separately.
Correct placement requires full release into the matching receiving region and a 2 second stable dwell. Full success requires all three cubes, no fall and no external intervention. A fall or invalid robot state terminates the episode. Score partial placements separately. Keep geometry, control rate and randomization ranges fixed across teams.
Metrics and comparison
Report correct cubes out of 90, full successes out of 30, falls, drops, retries and successful episode completion times. Evaluate the starting policy and final policy on the same seeds. For the human data ablation, use at least 10 matched held out seeds. Report absolute percentage point changes, sample counts and any compute differences. Improvement is an objective, not a promised consequence of fine tuning.
Track 1 rubric
Criterion
Points
Evidence
Autonomous sorting
25
25 × standard scene full task success fraction.
Generalization
25

World model use

Criterion
Points

Traceable extraction 10; valid robot supervision 10; data QA 5.
Post training evidence

Autonomous sorting
30
30 × full task success fraction across 30 final policy episodes.
Robustness and stability

Reproducibility and explanation

9 Prerequisites and participant preparation
These are advanced learning challenges. The preparation window should remove installation and hardware assembly as barriers while allowing participants to learn the task specific methods. Students are not expected to arrive with experience in every tool. Each team should collectively cover software development, basic machine learning and robot integration.
Topic
Minimum preparation
Provided support
Python and Git
Run scripts, manage environments, read logs and use version control.
Starter repository and environment smoke test.
Machine learning
Understand training and validation, loss, overfitting and pretrained models.
Small training exercise and checkpoint loading tutorial.
Robot geometry
Understand joints, grippers, frames, transforms and reachability.
Frame diagram, robot configuration and guided IK example.
Data handling
Understand synchronized episodes, labels, splits and dataset quality.
Sample episode, schema validator and visualization notebook.
Track 1 specifics
Teleoperate safely and explain action conditioned prediction.
Robot calibration workshop and compact world model example.
Track 2 specifics
Navigate Isaac, reset a task and understand human to robot retargeting.
Working humanoid scene, controller demo and example conversion pipeline.
Preparation sequence
Two weeks before: choose a track, form teams, receive documentation and request compute.
One week before: run the environment smoke test, load a sample dataset and execute a provided baseline.
Before opening: attend a 90 minute track workshop and a 30 minute evaluation briefing; complete hardware safety orientation for Track 1.
At event start: receive final starter data, seeded development scenes, submission templates and the frozen scoring rules.
What teams should learn during the event
Track 1 teams focus on useful learned dynamics, action selection, data diversity and calibration under scene changes. Track 2 teams focus on extracting transferable task information from video, generating valid embodiment specific supervision and measuring adaptation. Neither track requires developing a new foundation architecture from scratch.
Suggested team roles
Assign ownership for data and perception, model training, control and integration, and evaluation and reproducibility. Roles may overlap. Every team should reserve integration time instead of spending the entire event on isolated model experiments.
10 Organizer equipment and compute plan
Resource
Track 1
Track 2
Physical equipment
One leader and follower kit per team or a published shared access schedule; camera, clamps, bins, cubes, power and spare parts.
Phone or camera for demonstrations, simple props and an optional calibration target. A physical humanoid is not required.
Simulation and assets
Optional matching simulator for development; physical evaluation remains mandatory.
Working Isaac environment, humanoid asset, gripper or hand model, table, bins, cameras and reset scripts.
Compute planning
Start by testing compact dynamics models on a 16 to 24 GB GPU; larger pretrained models may need substantially more.
Reserve a supported RTX simulation machine and a training GPU. A 48 GB or larger training GPU is a planning starting point, not a guarantee for every GR00T recipe.
Host resources
Plan for 32 to 64 GB RAM and 100 GB free SSD per workstation, then profile the actual dataset and stack.
Plan for 64 GB RAM and 200 GB or more SSD; confirm simulator specific requirements on the chosen release.
Provision only after a dry run
The GPU figures above are organizer estimates. Before confirming capacity, run the actual pinned model, batch size, precision, optimizer, camera resolution and simulator concurrently or on separate machines as intended. Measure peak VRAM, training time, inference latency and disk consumption. Publish the tested configuration and a fair per team GPU hour quota.
Starter package required before launch
Pinned environment or container, installation instructions, license inventory and a one command smoke test.
Robot or humanoid configuration, camera and action schema, starter episodes and a working baseline rollout.
Training entry point, inference adapter, dataset validator, task resets, scoring script and sample results file.
For Track 1, a compact trainable world model template and a complete safe teleoperation example.
For Track 2, one end to end example from a short human clip to validated robot supervision and a small successful fine tuning run.
Development scene seeds, held out evaluation policy and clearly separated organizer only scoring state.
Launch acceptance gate
Do not open either track until a mentor can reproduce a baseline from a clean machine within the allocated resources. If the selected checkpoint cannot control the selected embodiment, resolve the adapter and action mapping before the event. Mentors should support setup and debugging while teams own the submitted learning pipeline.
11 Build schedule and submission requirements
Time
Track 1 milestone
Track 2 milestone
Hours 0 to 8
Calibrate, teleoperate, record starter episodes and run a baseline.
Run humanoid controllers, capture human clips and validate extraction.
Hours 8 to 24
Train dynamics, inspect predictions and integrate action selection.
Retarget or derive supervision; generate and validate robot episodes.
Hours 24 to 48
Run closed loop sorting and improve data coverage.
Adapt the checkpoint and complete autonomous sorting rollouts.
Hours 48 to 64
Test changed scenes, run ablations and investigate failures.
Run before and after tests, human data ablation and stability checks.
Hours 64 to 72
Freeze artifacts, verify reproducibility and prepare the demonstration.
Freeze artifacts, verify reproducibility and prepare the demonstration.
Required submission package
Source repository or source archive with a clear README, exact dependencies and commands for training, inference and evaluation.
Model weights or accessible checkpoint references with hashes, base model identity, licenses and training configuration.
Dataset manifest, representative permitted samples, train and test split definitions, provenance and collection consent statement.
Machine readable results with episode seed or scene ID, checkpoint, placements, full success, duration, interventions and termination reason.
A technical report of 4 to 6 pages describing architecture, data, learning objectives, experiments, failures and resource use.
A 3 to 5 minute demo video showing the full workflow; include one continuous autonomous rollout and one failure or recovery example.
Track specific evidence: predicted versus observed outcomes and action traces for Track 1; human clip to supervision lineage and before and after checkpoints for Track 2.
Live demonstration format
Allow 8 minutes per team: 2 minutes for the problem and architecture, 4 minutes for a live or supervised reproducible demonstration, and 2 minutes for judge questions. Official scoring uses the full trial protocol rather than a single selected demo. A pre recorded video may explain the system but cannot substitute for required reproducible runs.
Reproducibility check
Judges should be able to load the submitted checkpoint, reset a supplied scene and run inference using the documented commands. Teams must disclose manual calibration, external services, borrowed code, synthetic data, pre event work and any component that cannot be redistributed.
12 Fairness safety and organizer decisions
Fair access and evaluation integrity
Pretrained models and open source code are allowed with attribution and license compliance. Freeze the permitted base models, sensor options, compute budgets and starter datasets across teams. Track external API usage and cost if allowed. Do not provide test seeds, target coordinates or judge only simulator state as policy inputs. No gradient updates or new demonstrations are allowed after the scoring freeze.
Physical safety
Only trained operators may power or remount the arm. Provide an accessible stop mechanism, conservative speed and force limits, cable management and a clear exclusion zone. Keep hands outside the workspace during autonomy. Use lightweight objects and secure bins. Judges can stop unsafe motion immediately. Restart rules must be identical for all teams and distinguish equipment faults from algorithm failures.
Human recording and data use
Record consenting participants in an approved space. Frame hands and objects where possible. State who may access recordings, how long they will be retained and whether public release is optional. Teams retain their own work subject to the event terms and dependency licenses; organizers must publish those terms before registration.
Decisions to publish before registration
Decision
Recommended default
Duration and team size
72 hour event after a two week preparation window; 3 to 5 students.
Physical platform
SO 101 leader and follower or one tested equivalent; shared camera specification.
Humanoid and controllers
One tested Isaac compatible embodiment with working manipulation, standing and walking interfaces.
Model and simulator versions
Pinned GR00T N1.5 or N1.6, Isaac stack and dependency commits; optional approved AW 0 route.
Scene and calibration limits
Reachable regions, object dimensions, lighting bounds, mounting zones and relocation calibration procedure.
Resource access
Identical compute quotas, checkpoint availability, robot booking and mentor access rules.
Results and awards
Separate track rankings; optional awards for robust control, data pipeline and reproducibility.
Recommended completion targets
As non binding development goals, aim for at least 4 of 5 successful standard Track 1 trials and visible completion in changed scenes; for Track 2, aim for reproducible sorting and measurable improvement over the starting checkpoint. These targets are not eligibility gates or promised performance. Qualification depends on the required learning evidence and autonomous system, and ranking uses the published rubrics.
13 Technical references and glossary
These primary sources ground the tool and model descriptions. The task design, trial counts, scoring weights, hardware budgets and preparation schedule in this brief are proposed event rules. Organizers must verify availability, compatibility and licenses before distributing the final call for participation.
1 LeRobot repository
Robotics software, policies, datasets and hardware integrations.
https://github.com/huggingface/lerobot
2 SO 101 documentation
Leader and follower reference hardware, assembly and setup.
https://huggingface.co/docs/lerobot/so101
3 Agentic World Action Models paper
Research reference for predictive world action modeling with agentic planning.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30136
4 AW 0 official code
Implementation reference; inspect checkpoint, embodiment and compute requirements.
https://github.com/ZhuoyangLiu2005/agentic-wam
5 NVIDIA Isaac GR00T repository and releases
Model implementation and release history. Select the intended version rather than assuming the current main branch matches it.
https://github.com/NVIDIA/Isaac-GR00T
6 NVIDIA GR00T fine tuning playbook
Official N1.6 setup and adaptation guidance, including release alignment.
https://build.nvidia.com/playbooks/gr00t/instructions
7 NVIDIA Isaac Lab documentation
Simulation learning workflows, controllers, sensors and task construction.
https://isaac-sim.github.io/IsaacLab/main/index.html
Key terms
World model: a learned predictor of task relevant future state. World action model: a model combining future prediction with robot action modeling. Post training: adapting a pretrained model for an embodiment or task. Retargeting: converting human or reference motion into feasible robot motion. Proprioception: the robot’s internal state, such as joint positions. Ablation: a controlled comparison that removes one component to test its contribution.
Egocentric video: a first person view from the demonstrator. Exocentric video: a third person view. Domain randomization: deliberate variation of scene properties during training. Closed loop control: repeated observation and action adjustment during execution. IK: inverse kinematics, which maps an end effector target into joint configurations.
